title: Ugali portions that work for blood sugar control
body: You do not have to stop eating ugali. The key is portion size and what you eat it with. A fist-sized portion of ugali paired with a generous serving of sukuma wiki (collard greens) and a palm-sized piece of fish or chicken keeps your blood sugar steadier than a large ugali serving on its own. Cook the sukuma wiki with a small amount of oil rather than deep frying. Your family eats the same meal, just with different proportions on the plate.

title: Reducing salt without losing flavour
body: High salt intake raises blood pressure, but bland food is not the answer. Replace half your usual salt with a squeeze of lemon juice, diced tomatoes, or dhania (coriander). When making stew, add garlic and ginger early in the cooking process for deeper flavour. These ingredients are available at any local market for under KES 50. Your whole family benefits from lower sodium, not just you.

title: Smart swaps at the market
body: When shopping at the market, choose sweet potatoes over white potatoes. They have a lower glycaemic index, meaning they raise blood sugar more slowly. Brown chapati flour (atta mark 1) costs about the same as refined flour but releases sugar more gradually. Buy seasonal fruits like mangoes and pawpaw instead of juice boxes, which contain concentrated sugar without the fibre that slows absorption.

title: Drinking enough water on a busy day
body: Dehydration makes blood thicker, which raises blood pressure and makes it harder for your kidneys to clear waste. Keep a water bottle with you and aim for 6-8 glasses per day. If plain water feels boring, add slices of lemon or cucumber. Avoid sodas and sweetened juices. They add sugar and calories without quenching thirst. Tea and coffee count toward your fluid intake, but limit sugar to one teaspoon or less.

title: Walking after meals lowers blood sugar
body: A 15-minute walk after your main meal can reduce your blood sugar spike by up to 30%. You do not need a gym or special equipment. Walk around your neighbourhood, to the local duka, or even up and down your compound. If mobility is limited, try seated leg raises or gentle arm movements while sitting. The goal is consistent daily movement, not intense exercise.

title: Safe exercise when you have high blood pressure
body: Regular moderate exercise lowers blood pressure by 5-8 mmHg over time. Aim for 30 minutes most days. Walking, cycling, and swimming are excellent choices. Avoid heavy lifting or exercises where you hold your breath and strain (like pushing heavy furniture). If you feel dizzy, have chest pain, or get a severe headache during exercise, stop immediately and rest. Start slowly and build up gradually.

title: Myth: Diabetes can be cured with herbal remedies
body: There is no herbal cure for diabetes. Some traditional remedies like bitter gourd (karela) and cinnamon may have a small effect on blood sugar, but they cannot replace prescribed medication. Stopping your diabetes medication in favour of herbal treatments puts you at serious risk of dangerously high blood sugar, which can damage your kidneys, eyes, and nerves over time. If you want to try a herbal supplement, tell your doctor first so they can check for dangerous interactions.

title: Myth: You can stop blood pressure medication when you feel fine
body: High blood pressure is called the silent killer because you usually cannot feel it. Feeling fine does not mean your blood pressure is normal. It means the medication is working. Stopping suddenly can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure, increasing your risk of stroke or heart attack. If you are concerned about side effects or cost, talk to your doctor about alternatives. Never stop on your own.

title: It is normal to feel overwhelmed
body: Managing a long-term health condition is exhausting. Some days you will feel motivated, other days you will not want to think about medications, diet, or doctor visits. That is completely normal. You are not failing. The fact that you are here, reading this, means you are doing something for your health today. Talk to someone you trust about how you feel. Holding it all inside makes the burden heavier. A pharmacist, a friend, or a family member can help carry the weight.

title: Living well with a lifelong condition
body: Receiving a diagnosis that requires ongoing treatment changes how you see your future. Some people feel angry, others feel ashamed, and some try to ignore it altogether. None of these reactions are wrong. What matters is what happens next. Millions of people across Kenya live full, active lives while managing their health. You are not defined by a condition. You are defined by how you respond to it. Start small. One refill at a time. One walk at a time. One day at a time.

title: When and how to check your blood sugar at home
body: If you have a glucometer, check your blood sugar first thing in the morning before eating (fasting reading) and 2 hours after your largest meal. Write down the numbers or use a simple notebook. A fasting reading between 4-7 mmol/L (72-126 mg/dL) is generally good for type 2 diabetes. After meals, aim for below 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL). Bring your notebook to your next doctor visit. Patterns matter more than single readings.

title: One month of consistent refills
body: You have refilled your medication on time for a full month. That consistency is protecting your health in ways you cannot always feel but are very real. Every dose taken on time keeps your blood levels stable, reduces your risk of complications, and means fewer emergency visits down the road. Keep it up. Your next milestone is three months of consistent refills.
